The first thing the town forgot was the name of the river.

Not the river itself. It still moved behind the bakery, green in the morning and copper at dusk. Children still threw sticks into it from the bridge. But one Tuesday, when a stranger asked what it was called, nobody could answer.

“Everyone knows that,” said the baker, and then stood silently with flour on his wrists.

By Thursday, the name had vanished from the maps. There was no blank space where it should have been. The letters had rearranged themselves into the thin blue line of the water.

This worried Mara less than it worried most people. She repaired clocks for a living and was accustomed to things failing in ways their owners considered impossible.

“It was working yesterday,” they always told her.

“Yes,” she always said. “That is usually how it happens.”

Her shop stood between a florist and an empty building that everyone remembered differently. Some recalled a butcher. Others insisted it had sold shoes. An elderly man came every December to post a letter through its sealed door.

When Mara asked him why, he said, “Because she might come back.”

Then the town forgot the color yellow.

Sunflowers became difficult to describe. Mustard was identified by its taste. The florist spent an afternoon weeping among bouquets she could arrange perfectly well but could no longer explain.

People continued to see the color. That was the peculiar part. They knew something distinguished a lemon from a lime, beyond shape and flavor, but their thoughts slid away whenever they tried to name it.

The mayor organized a meeting.

“We must preserve what remains,” she announced.

A committee began writing everything down.

They recorded street names, recipes, birthdays, the proper method for folding fitted sheets. They interviewed grandparents. They measured the fountain. They described the smell of rain on the railway platform.

By morning, half their notebooks contained only patient, evenly spaced dots.

Mara did not attend the second meeting. A clock had arrived without a customer.

It stood on her workbench when she unlocked the shop: a small brass carriage clock, warm to the touch, with thirteen marks around its face. Instead of hands, it held a narrow window through which she could see a room.

Inside the room, a woman was peeling an apple.

Mara leaned closer.

The woman’s knife moved in a slow spiral. The peel lengthened, curling toward the floor. Somewhere beyond the edges of the window, a child laughed.

Mara knew that laugh.

She sat down hard.

Her mother had died thirty years earlier. The kitchen had been demolished twenty years earlier. Yet there was the chipped blue bowl, the loose cupboard hinge, the afternoon light on her mother’s forearm.

On the underside of the clock, someone had scratched a sentence:

**Nothing is lost while someone is willing to keep it.**

Mara watched until nightfall.

The next morning, the town forgot how to whistle.

Men pursed their lips at dogs and produced embarrassed breaths. A kettle boiled in the café while three people stared at it, troubled by a sound they recognized but could not imitate.

Mara turned the clock over and examined its screws.

There were none.

She tapped the case, tested the seams, held it against her ear. Instead of ticking, she heard someone walking through fallen leaves.

At noon, she carried it to the river.

The stranger who had asked the river’s name was sitting beneath the bridge.

He wore an ordinary coat. His shoes were muddy. Beside him lay a suitcase tied with string.

“You left something in my shop,” Mara said.

“I leave it wherever someone might understand.”

“What is happening here?”

The stranger looked at the water.

“Your town is becoming very good at remembering.”

“That is the opposite of what is happening.”

“Is it?”

He opened the suitcase.

Inside were a red mitten, a cracked saucer, seven keys, a theater ticket, and a small wooden horse missing one leg.

Mara waited.

He picked up the mitten and held it carefully.

“My daughter dropped this on the way to school. I found it coming home from work. That evening, I meant to give it back.”

“Why didn’t you?”

“I kept putting it off.”

He placed it beside the saucer.

“The clock lets me visit that evening. There are other evenings too. After a while, I stopped looking for anything it couldn’t show me.”

Mara thought of her shop, its stopped clocks waiting on shelves. She had missed two meals watching her mother peel the apple. Outside, customers had knocked and gone away.

“Why bring it here?”

“I thought a clockmaker could stop it.”

Mara returned to her shop and placed the clock on the bench.

Her mother was still peeling the apple.

But now Mara noticed how little there was to see beyond the table. The doorway opened onto darkness. No wind stirred the curtain. Her mother never looked up.

She reached for her smallest screwdriver.

The brass yielded beneath it like wax.

Inside, there were no gears. Only thousands of tiny folded papers.

She unfolded one.

The river’s name.

Another held a sharp, cheerful whistle. A third opened in her fingers with the brightness of marigolds.

Mara opened the shop door.

All night, she unfolded papers and let them go.

They drifted down the street, caught in hedges, slipped beneath doors. One landed on the mayor’s windowsill. Another dissolved against a sleeping child’s cheek.

Near dawn, Mara found the last paper.

It was warm.

She knew what it contained before she opened it: the kitchen, the apple, her mother alive in afternoon light.

For a long time, she held it.

Then she unfolded it.

There was no revelation. Her mother did not speak. The paper simply lifted from her palm and disappeared through the open door.

In the morning, the florist brought yellow tulips.

Someone whistled on the bridge.

Mara ate breakfast beside her workbench. She could still remember her mother’s hands, though not quite the shape of the knife.

At nine, a customer arrived with a broken watch.

Mara let him in.
